\chapter{Beautiful, and Not}
\label{ch:ml-beauty}
\hlchaptermodality{97}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is beautiful, name beauty itself, and deny it.}

From cold: both ends of one quality, and which letter arrives when aaNu follows a word.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sundaraṁ]{\ml{സുന്ദരം} (sundaraṁ) — beautiful}

\label{lesson:ML-C97-sundaram}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is easy}. You built that sentence one chapter ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} — \emph{sundaraṁ} — \textbf{beautiful.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ sundaramāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is beautiful.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Read what you did there.} The word ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, so it welds onto \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} the way the last chapter's two words did, and you did it without being told.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}} & this is easy \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{പ്രയാസമാണ്}} & this is difficult \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} & this is beautiful \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is what a frame is for. \textbf{The chapter before this one cost you a rule; this one cost you a word}, and the weld came free.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sundaraṁ}
  \item \emph{itŭ sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item the same sentence about something being easy
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{beautiful}? (\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}}.) Did you need a new rule to say \emph{this is beautiful}? (\textbf{No} — it ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, like \textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}} and \textbf{\ml{പ്രയാസം}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhaṁgi]{\ml{ഭംഗി} (bhaṁgi) — beauty}

\label{lesson:ML-C97-bhangi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is beautiful}. Then say \emph{child} — you have had that word a long time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} — \emph{bhaṁgi} — \textbf{beauty.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{ഭംഗിയാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ bhaṁgiyāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is beautiful.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Read the gloss again. The word means \emph{beauty}, but the sentence does \textbf{not} say \emph{this is beauty} — it says \textbf{this is beautiful}, and it is the way you are most likely to hear it said.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Two different things are happening here, and only one of them is new.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} & the \textbf{m} was already there \\
\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{ഭംഗിയാണ്}} & a \textbf{\ml{യ}} is genuinely added \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

In \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} nothing is added at all. The \textbf{\ml{ം}} is the sound \textbf{m}, and it stays; only its \emph{writing} moves, because the bare sign cannot carry a vowel. \textbf{You were told that last chapter.}

\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി} is the other case}, and you have met the reason before. It ends in a vowel, \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} begins with one, and Malayalam will not let two vowels sit together — so a \textbf{\ml{യ}} slides in between them. \textbf{The joining chapter said exactly that} about \textbf{\ml{അരിയും}}.

What is new is only where it happens. \textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{കുട്ടിയാണ്}} — \emph{this is my child} — has the same \textbf{\ml{യ}}, for the same reason.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhaṁgi}, then \emph{bhaṁgiyāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{sundaraṁ}, then \emph{sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item which of the two actually gained a sound, and which only changed its spelling
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{beauty}? (\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}}.) Why does a \textbf{\ml{യ}} come in before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{Two vowels will not sit together}.) Is anything added in \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}}? (\textbf{No} — that \textbf{m} was already there.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[itŭ sundaramalla]{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല} (itŭ sundaramalla) — this is not beautiful}

\label{lesson:ML-C97-alla-sundaram}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is beautiful}. Then say the word that denies being what you were called.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the denial welds too}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല}.} — \emph{itŭ sundaramalla} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is not beautiful.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{You already know how that was built.} \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} is the negative of \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}, and it welds on the same way:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം} + \ml{ആണ്}} & \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} — this is beautiful \\
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം} + \ml{അല്ല}} & \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല}} — this is not beautiful \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same \textbf{\ml{മ}}, same reason: the \textbf{m} was always there and now has a vowel after it, so it is written with the full letter.

\textbf{When you first met \ml{അല്ല} it was written apart} — \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അധ്യാപകൻ} \ml{അല്ല}}, \emph{I am not a teacher.} \textbf{That was a choice about writing, not a different grammar.} Weld them and you get \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{അധ്യാപകനല്ല}} — \emph{ñān adhyāpakanalla} — which is as ordinary as the other.

And look at what the \textbf{\ml{ൻ}} does there. \textbf{You were shown this at \ml{അധ്യാപകനെ}}: the chillu is the shape a consonant takes \textbf{at the end of a word}, so once anything follows it the full letter comes back — \textbf{\ml{ൻ} $\to$ \ml{ന}}. It happens here too: \textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{മകനാണ്}}, \emph{this is my son}.

\textbf{Do not carry that across to the \ml{ം}.} The chillu goes back to its letter whatever follows it; the \textbf{\ml{ം}} does different things for different endings, as you saw last chapter. What the two share is only this one join.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both ends of the same line, from one new word and one you already had.

This is how the far end of most qualities will arrive for a while: \textbf{not by a second word, but by denying the first one.} It is what a learner can build today, and it is what a speaker often says anyway.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{itŭ sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{itŭ sundaramalla}
  \item the two one after the other, and hear where they part
  \item which letter \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} and \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല}} share in the middle, and why
  \item \emph{ñān adhyāpakanalla}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \emph{this is not beautiful}? (\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല}}.) Does \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} weld on the way \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} does? (\textbf{Yes} — same \textbf{\ml{മ}}, same reason.) What does the \textbf{\ml{ൻ}} of \textbf{\ml{അധ്യാപകൻ}} do when it welds? (\textbf{It goes back to \ml{ന}} — as in \textbf{\ml{മകനാണ്}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sundaravuṁ allāthatuṁ enna ōrmma]{(beautiful, and not) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R97-beauty-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{this is beautiful}, then deny it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two different events}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{joined to \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}} & \textbf{what happened} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}} & \textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}} & the \textbf{m} was already there \\
\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} & \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}} & the \textbf{m} was already there \\
\textbf{\ml{കുട്ടി}} & \textbf{\ml{കുട്ടിയാണ്}} & a \textbf{\ml{യ}} was added \\
\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} & \textbf{\ml{ഭംഗിയാണ്}} & a \textbf{\ml{യ}} was added \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The two halves are not the same event.} In the top pair nothing is added — the \textbf{m} was always in the word, and only its writing moves once a vowel sits behind it. In the bottom pair a \textbf{\ml{യ}} genuinely appears, because the word ends in a vowel and two vowels will not sit together.

And \textbf{what attaches matters too}, not only how the word ended: the same \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}} gives \textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരവും}} when the \emph{and} ending arrives.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമാണ്}.} — this is beautiful.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല}.} — this is not beautiful.
\end{quote}

The second is not a second word. \textbf{\ml{അല്ല}} is the negative of \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} and welds the same way — \textbf{same \ml{മ}, same reason.}

So one new quality gave you both ends of a line. That is how the far end of most qualities will arrive for a while — \textbf{by denying the near one}, which is both what you can build today and what a speaker often says anyway.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sundaraṁ} $\to$ \emph{sundaramāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{bhaṁgi} $\to$ \emph{bhaṁgiyāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{itŭ sundaramalla}
  \item which of the four joined forms actually gained a sound, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Beautiful, and beauty? (\textbf{\ml{സുന്ദരം}, \ml{ഭംഗി}}.) Which of the two gains a sound before \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}? (\textbf{\ml{ഭംഗി}} — a \textbf{\ml{യ}}.) And how do you deny it? (\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{സുന്ദരമല്ല}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
